title: A means to annotate redundant links
body:
I realize that this very much sounds like an X-Y problem. Maybe it is, but I think I have found a narrow gap among existing solutions that justifies this request along with enough use cases for it to be more widely useful. Below, there's a short version where I jump to the point followed by a long version where I try to show the edge cases that led me to posting this. # Short version Screen readers have a mode that lists just the links on a page. For various reasons (not all correct), links to the same location are often listed multiple times on the same page. These duplicate links may be important in the context of the page but are redundant when the page is treated as a directory of links. I would like an attribute that marks such links as redundant, causing them to be skipped by screen readers when listing all links but otherwise treated normally. # Long version I'm going to present two use cases. The first is common and can be worked around with enough effort. The second is less common and really doesn't have any good solutions that I have been able to figure out. This is a common (quite flawed) pattern ```html

{{ title }}

{{ teaser-text }} Read more
``` There is a lot wrong with that! There's 3 identical links—with no text, the article title, and the not very meaningful "Read more"—and the image mysteriously gets its own tab stop. The first two links could be fixed with ```html

{{ title }}

 ``` Wrapping the image and the header in one link makes both clickable, and removes the weird tab stop on the image, but it also makes the link a block level element. This has its own downsides, like making what appears to be inert whitespace into a clickable area and making it more difficult to select text. With some CSS that can be fixed up in most situations, depending on the end layout. Another way to handle this is kind of awful: ```html

{{ title }}

``` That takes the img out of the tab order and hides it from screen readers while still allowing a mouse/finger to hit it. Normally that's a terrible idea but its proximity to and redundancy with the actual link absolves some of its sins. That said, it's probably still a bad idea for reasons I haven't considered—and I'm not recommending it. One of those is necessary since the link needs meaningful text and it's not good for anyone to have redundant links back-to-back like that. Either of those solutions still leaves the redundant "Read more". By itself, it violates WCAG and needs to be turned into something like ```html Read more about {{title}} ``` That makes it work locally, and would need to be done regardless, but it's still has the problem that when a screen reader when listing links will announce—X, read more about X, Y, read more about Y, Z, read more about Z. Less than ideal, though better than: X, read more, Y, read more, Z, read more. It should just be: X, Y, Z. The best solution to this that I've seen is https://www.sarasoueidan.com/blog/nested-links/ but that still has the trade off where the entire `article` is a big rectangular, unselectable link. It would be nicer to just tack an attribute on the read more link so that it worked as intended without interfering with the read all links mode of screen readers, but I could live with the status quo here. As a developer, there are workarounds even if they have some undesirable trade offs. I am, if anything, more annoyed as a user by my inability to select text or finding that an errant mouse click has taken me to a page that I did not intend to visit as this pattern becomes more common and gets used in places where the design makes it less clear where the blocks begin and end. It's in a less common related case that I found no good solutions: a large glossary-style page with lots of cross-indexing. I made this a long time ago and embarrassed by the design and numerous a11y issues: https://jimmyfrasche.github.io/go-reflection-codex/ I've been working on an update (the structure is largely identical so the above link suffices for discussion). I've managed to make it much more pleasant and accessible over all, except in screen readers when listing all links. Most of the links on that page are redundant but also necessary. If I had a way to mark links as redundant, I would do so for the majority of the links on the page. They're all important but most are only important in context. Listing all links on the page should just list: the skip links, the links in the prefatory text, the links in the table of context, and the links in the footer. They're the canonical links. Even if I split this page into one page per article, I'd still have this issue unless I removed the By Topic and By Use indices or the first page just had links for which index to go to. That's too many clicks for too little text and makes it harder to explore. Even if I removed the additional top-level indices and the per-article cross-references, I'd still have the problem with the "back to top" links. I could make it a single fixed link that sits in the corner of the viewport, but then it's removed from the natural tab order so it wouldn't work well for keyboard users, essentially defeating the purpose. The only solution I could think of is to make my own redundant link attribute, say `data-redundant`, then have a script rewrite all `a[data-redundant]` with something that looks and acts like a link but only gets `role=link` when focused so it behaves like a link in all cases but does not get listed with all links (I'm assuming that an interactive element with `role=link` would normally get listed by most screen readers along with the proper links). I'm trepidatious about going down that path. There's a lot that could go wrong that could escape my ability to test, and, if anything does, the majority of the links on the page are broken. That doesn't seem like a risk worth taking in this case given how fundamental links are and how prevalent redundant links are on that page, though the idea may be useful as the basis of a polyfill. It seems like there should be a better way to handle this and that a better way would have uses in more common scenarios, as well.
